title: GNN-as-Judge: LLMs and Graph Structure Together
one_liner: When an LLM and a graph-structure model disagree on which nodes matter, their disagreement becomes a signal for which labels to trust.
lead: Large language models are good at understanding text, but they struggle when text sits inside a graph with few labeled examples. This paper shows how to use a simpler model, one that respects the graph's structure, to identify which unlabeled nodes should get labels first, then harvest both agreement and disagreement between the two models to build a reliable set of training examples.

problem.h2: Why LLMs alone fail on graph data with few labels
paras: A language model reads text and guesses a label. If you have only a handful of labeled examples, you need more. A naive approach: feed the model more unlabeled node texts, let it predict labels for them, then use those predictions as training data. This is called pseudo-labeling.

This breaks in two ways. First, when only a few nodes are labeled, the model has almost no context and makes wild guesses on which nodes matter. It labels nodes that are noise-adjacent to the labeled ones, because it has no way to know if a node is actually connected to the labeled examples or just floating in the text space. Second, when you fine-tune the language model on these noisy pseudo-labels, the model memorizes the mistakes, and the errors get locked in.

callout.html: Use a graph-structure model to identify which unlabeled nodes are actually close to labeled ones, then watch where the language model and the graph model agree or disagree, and only trust labels at those disagreement points.

steps.text: Graph model scores which unlabeled nodes sit next to labeled ones.
Language model assigns each node a label and a confidence score.
Where graph says close but LLM is uncertain, or LLM is confident but graph says far.
Label nodes where the two models most disagree. Trust those labels.
Use only the high-agreement, high-signal pseudo-labels. Teach the language model structure.

object.h2: What the paper changes: which nodes get pseudo-labels
paras: The paper does not change the models themselves. It changes the ORDER and SELECTION of which unlabeled nodes get assigned labels for retraining. Instead of labeling all nodes or picking randomly, it labels first at points of high disagreement between the two models.

hidden.name: graph-text disagreement
paras: The paper measures a NEW quantity: how much the graph model and the language model disagree on a given node. The graph model computes a score for how close a node sits to the labeled part of the graph (neighbors of labeled nodes score high; isolated nodes score low). The language model computes a confidence for its predicted label. A node with high graph-closeness but low LLM-confidence is a HIGH DISAGREEMENT node — this is where to assign a label first.

The paper estimates this by combining the graph-nearness score (how far a node sits from labeled ones, measured by the graph structure) with the LLM confidence (how sure the language model is of its guess). When the graph says a node is close but the LLM is uncertain, that is a high-disagreement spot where structural information might correct the LLM.

heat.caption: Darker means higher disagreement (graph close, LLM uncertain). Marked cells labeled first.

reads.html: A node's disagreement score tells you how much structural context the LLM is missing on that node. High disagreement means the graph has information the text does not.
The paper uses disagreement to rank which pseudo-labels are most informative. It labels high-disagreement nodes first, treating them as ground truth during fine-tuning.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: structural insight corrects text-only blindness
paras: A language model trained on text alone has no idea which nodes matter to each other. It sees isolated snippets of text and guesses labels based on the words. A graph model, by contrast, knows which nodes are neighbors and propagates information along edges. It cannot read text, but it knows structure.

When the two models DISAGREE on a structurally close node — the graph says this node is a neighbor of labeled nodes, but the LLM is uncertain — that is a spot where the graph's structural knowledge could help the LLM. By labeling there first (giving the LLM a true example it can learn from), the LLM learns to associate node closeness with label patterns. Over time, as more pseudo-labels accumulate, the LLM begins to encode the structure into its own predictions.

The second part is noise reduction. Not all pseudo-labels are reliable. The paper uses a weakly-supervised fine-tuning loss: instead of treating pseudo-labels as hard truth, it treats them as soft signals. Nodes with high disagreement are trusted more; nodes where both models agree are de-weighted. This way, even if some pseudo-labels are wrong, the fine-tuning process does not lock in the mistakes.

stages.s: Few labeled nodes, many unlabeled text nodes on a graph
Graph model scores node closeness to labeled part
LLM predicts labels and confidence for all nodes
Compute disagreement: close nodes with low LLM confidence
Pseudo-label high-disagreement nodes, weight by confidence
Fine-tune LLM on weighted pseudo-labels, learn structure

math.words: To rank which unlabeled nodes to label first, compute a score that combines graph closeness and LLM confidence disagreement. Higher score means label first.
symbols: ranking score for node i (higher means label this node first)
how certain the LLM is of its prediction for node i (0 to 1, from softmax output)
how close node i sits to labeled nodes (0 to 1, from graph-diffusion score)

worked.title: Tiny worked example
lines: Node A: LLM confidence 0.6, graph closeness 0.9 -> score = (1 - 0.6) * 0.9 = 0.4 * 0.9 = 0.36
Node B: LLM confidence 0.9, graph closeness 0.8 -> score = (1 - 0.9) * 0.8 = 0.1 * 0.8 = 0.08
Node C: LLM confidence 0.5, graph closeness 0.7 -> score = (1 - 0.5) * 0.7 = 0.5 * 0.7 = 0.35
Node A scores highest (0.36). It is close to labeled nodes but the LLM is unsure. Label Node A first.

math.note: Nodes where the graph says close but the LLM is uncertain score highest and get labeled first, because these are spots where structural knowledge can most help.

charts.title: Baseline: LLM alone with random pseudo-labels
charts.note: Random pseudo-labels teach bad patterns. Fine-tuning memorizes the noise.

charts.title: This paper: GNN-as-Judge with structured pseudo-labels
charts.note: Structured pseudo-labels are trustworthy. LLM learns graph patterns because training on high-disagreement examples teaches it to associate neighbor closeness with label consistency, a pattern it sees nowhere else and thus learns to rely on.

items.b: Graph structure is missing or noisy.
items.html: If the edges in the graph do not actually reflect true relationships (links are random or mislabeled), the GNN closeness scores mean nothing. The paper assumes edges are correct. If edges are wrong, pseudo-labels will be ranked wrong.

items.b: LLM is already very confident everywhere.
items.html: If the language model assigns high confidence to all nodes, there is little disagreement to signal on. The ranking becomes flat, and pseudo-labels are chosen almost randomly. Works only if the LLM is uncertain in at least some regions.

items.b: Weak labels in the seed set.
items.html: The whole method rests on the initial few labeled examples being correct. If the seed labels are wrong, the graph model propagates those mistakes, and disagreement becomes noise. The initial labeled set must be clean.

When you pick examples where one model sees structure but the other is blind, you teach the blind model (the LLM) to notice what the structural model sees. This is a genuine transfer of knowledge, not just noise reduction.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small text graph (e.g., 50 nodes, each with a short text description). Hand-label 5 nodes (say, red/blue categories based on their text). Run the GNN model and the LLM model separately. Compute the disagreement score for each unlabeled node. Pseudo-label the top 10 highest-disagreement nodes according to the paper's algorithm. Then fine-tune the LLM on those 10 pseudo-labels (and the original 5). Measure accuracy on a held-out test set (e.g., 20 nodes you labeled but hid from training). Compare against: (1) LLM trained only on the original 5 labeled nodes, and (2) LLM trained on 15 random pseudo-labels. The paper's method should show higher final accuracy than both baselines.
demo.closing: The demo proves that disagreement-ranked pseudo-labels beat random selection, because structure + text together guide the LLM better than text alone.
